justification: None of the provided articles examine epilepsy at all. The Parkinson's study (PMID 20035503) lists TRAPPC4 as differentially expressed in substantia nigra neurons but the associated variant found was in PDXK, not TRAPPC4, and the phenotype is Parkinson disease, not epilepsy. The smallpox vaccine eQTL study (PMID 27052692) involves TRAPPC4 in an apoptosis-related epistatic interaction regulating gene expression in an immune context, with no neurological phenotype. The microwave exposure study (PMID 26383594) is a mouse brain expression screen concerning learning and memory, not epilepsy, and does not implicate TRAPPC4 variants. A small amount of weight is retained for "Hypothesized" because of generic brain-expression/vesicle-transport biology, but there is no logical basis connecting TRAPPC4 to epilepsy in this literature set.

justification: No article in this set reports LRRTM2 variants identified in autism probands or families; the only human sequencing study (PMID 23326251) screened 330 ID/DD patients and found no relevant LRRTM2 alterations, and its 5q31 microdeletion spans multiple genes (CTNNA1, LRRTM2), so it cannot single out LRRTM2. The remaining literature is biochemical, structural, or mouse/in vitro work establishing LRRTM2 as a postsynaptic neurexin ligand that organizes excitatory synapses (PMIDs 20519524, 30262834, 29784826, 24005312, 30100184), with autism relevance asserted only as background via the neurexin–neuroligin pathway (PMIDs 21155806, 24587117). NRXN2/NRXN1 truncating mutations in ASD patients (PMID 21424692) implicate the pathway and use LRRTM2 binding as a functional assay, but the causal variants are in neurexins, not LRRTM2. This fits "Hypothesized": strong, directly relevant biology and pathway/animal-model data without human genetic variant evidence. A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" in case the multi-gene 5q31 deletion/ID candidacy is credited, and to "Novel" given the explicitly negative mutation screen.

justification: All provided articles concern MYH2 as a skeletal muscle myosin heavy chain IIa gene causing hereditary myosin myopathies with ophthalmoplegia, congenital contractures, dysphagia and muscle weakness (e.g., PMIDs 11114175, 20418530, 24193343, 23388406, 28729039); none report autism spectrum disorder phenotypes or ASD cohorts. The only tangential mentions are a single Chinese case report of motor developmental delay with intellectual disability and MYH2 variants (PMID 30662633), a WES study of suspected mitochondrial disease listing MYH2 among neuromuscular findings (PMID 30009132), and a neural tube defect DNA methylation study where MYH2 hypermethylation was observed (PMID 28059605) — none of these constitute evidence of an ASD association, and intellectual disability or neural tube defects are not established ASD precursors attributable to this gene. There are no human genetic studies linking MYH2 variants to ASD, and no mechanistic or animal data connecting this fast-twitch muscle myosin to autism biology. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small residual allowance for a weak biological/neurodevelopmental hypothesis arising from the isolated ID case report.

justification: All the provided literature concerns CHRNA1 as the muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor alpha1 subunit, with variants causing congenital myasthenic syndromes, fetal akinesia deformation sequence/multiple pterygium syndrome, and polymorphisms associated with autoimmune myasthenia gravis. None of these papers reports seizures, epilepsy, or any CNS excitability phenotype linked to CHRNA1 variants; the gene product is expressed at the neuromuscular junction rather than in central neuronal circuits (unlike the neuronal CHRNA4/CHRNB2 genes in epilepsy). There are no human genetic association studies, functional neuronal data, or animal models in this set that link CHRNA1 to epilepsy. The co-mentions are entirely incidental to epilepsy, so the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a small residual probability for a hypothesized cholinergic-pathway rationale.

justification: No article in this set reports GRIA2 sequence variants identified in autism patients. The autism-relevant human genetic findings concern other genes whose products act on GluA2: GRIP1 missense variants in an autism cohort that alter GluA2 recycling/surface distribution (PMID 21383172) and EPAC2/RAPGEF4 variants that modulate GluR2/3 removal from spines (PMIDs 19734897, 21115118) — these implicate GluA2 biology, not GRIA2 variation. Human GRIA2 variant/CNV reports here are tied to intellectual disability or complex 4q32 deletions spanning many genes (PMIDs 22669415, 20358617, 19623214), which cannot single out GRIA2 and do not address ASD directly; other GRIA2 association studies address schizophrenia, lithium response, depression, and methamphetamine dependence. Supporting mechanistic links come from animal work (VPA rat model with GluA2-containing AMPAR removal, PMID 28733898; MeCP2/CP-AMPAR seizure model, PMID 29738885; MTHFR mouse synaptic composition, PMID 26235956), which places the evidence in the Hypothesized tier. A minority of weight is left for Existing given the convergent GluA2-centred human findings in ASD cohorts, but these are variants in partner genes rather than GRIA2 itself.

justification: The original discovery study (PMID 25401298) identified the recurrent de novo KCNC1 c.959G>A (p.Arg320His) variant in 11 unrelated exome-sequenced probands plus 2 additional affected individuals with progressive myoclonus epilepsy, with functional dominant-negative validation. This was independently replicated and expanded in a cohort of 20 MEAK patients with detailed electroclinical phenotyping (PMID 28380698) and in familial cases with maternal somatic mosaicism (PMID 29428275). Supporting functional work in human-derived channel expression systems (PMIDs 29894724, 27629860) confirms loss of function, and additional reports describe treatment responses in a KCNC1-mutated patient (PMID 28166365). The allelic series also includes a nonsense variant causing intellectual disability without seizures (PMID 28145425), refining the phenotype spectrum but not undermining the epilepsy link. Multiple independent human probands and families thus establish causation.
